newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Dhaka, Delhi agree on sub-regional trade bloc.
newsitem.headline: Dhaka, Delhi agree on sub-regional trade bloc.

text.p: Bangladesh and India, enjoying warmer relations since signing a landmark water-sharing treaty last month, agreed on Tuesday to create a sub-regional grouping to foster economic cooperation in South Asia.

Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda unveiled plans in Dhaka on Tuesday for the grouping, within the framework of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).
The SAARC groups Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Maldives, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

"Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and the regions of India immediately contiguous to us could very fruitfully and meaningfully enter into immediate cooperation in vitally important areas," Hasina told a joint news conference before Deve Gowda left Dhaka after a two-day visit.
"This (new grouping) will only be supplementary to SAARC. It is for faster track development within the SAARC with a sub-regional approach," she said.
The SAARC so far has been largely ineffective mainly due to militant rivalry between India and Pakistan.

Gowda arrived in Bangladesh on Monday, less than a month after the two countries ended a decades-old dispute by signing an accord to share water from the Ganges River, which flows through India and Bangladesh.
The two prime ministers said they had agreed to boost trade and work on resolving issues such as cross-border insurgencies and sharing water from common rivers.
Apart from the Ganges, 53 other rivers flow through the two countries before reaching the Bay of Bengal.
"Issues pending (between the two countries) will be solved without an iota of suspicion," Gowda told the new conference.
He said India would allow tariff concessions on 500 Bangladeshi items from March, enabling Bangladesh to boost exports to India.
A widening bilateral trade gap has been a major concern to Bangladesh. In 1995/96 (July-June), Bangladesh imported $1.1 billion in goods from India but exports were only $70 million, officials said.
The Indian leader said the Bangladesh-India Joint Economic Commission (JEC) would meet in March to explore further economic cooperation.
Asked whether the countries reached consensus on a previous Indian proposal for a trading route through Bangladesh, Deve Gowda said the issue could be discussed at the JEC meeting.
India has long been pressing Bangladesh for a trade corridor to transport goods to its hilly northeastern states.
The two leaders said a joint working group would meet by the end of January to map out strategies to combat insurgencies and other cross-border crimes.
"We are committed and determined as friendliest neighbouring countries to eliminate any kind of terrorism or insurgency that may affect our respective national interest," Hasina said.
India has long faced problems in its northeast, bordering Bangladesh, Burma and China.
Tribal insurgents in Bangladesh have been fighting a bush war since 1973 for autonomy in the 5,500 sq mile (14,200 sq km) Chittagong Hill Tracts bordering India and Burma.
